question: Why do healthcare workers and scientists use microbial taxonomy?

options.A: To invent new antibiotics for resistant bacteria
options.B: To measure the exact weight of a viral particle
options.C: To destroy all microbes found in clinical samples
options.D: To name, describe, and group microorganisms logically

explanation: Think of taxonomy like a filing system for tiny living things! It helps us organize, name, and group microbes so we can easily identify them and treat infections correctly. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h1)

question: What do we call the specific part of taxonomy that focuses on giving organisms their formal scientific names?
explanation: Nomenclature is just the fancy scientific word for the rules we use to name things. Think 'nomen' equals name! [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h1)

question: In biological classification, which rank sits right at the very top as the broadest category?
explanation: Domain is the biggest group of all, splitting all cellular life into broad categories like Bacteria and Eukarya. You've got this! [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h2)

question: A standard scientific name for a microbe uses a two-part naming system. Which two levels make up this name?
explanation: You'll often see this in textbooks, like Escherichia coli—where Escherichia is the genus and coli is the species! [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h2)

question: After a Gram stain in the lab, what color do Gram-positive bacteria show under the microscope?
explanation: Gram-positive bacteria have thick cell walls that hold onto the purple stain tightly. A great little fact to keep in your nursing toolkit! [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h3)

question: A lab report mentions spherical bacteria growing in grapelike clusters. What is the correct term for this shape and arrangement?
explanation: Staphylo means a cluster (like a bunch of grapes), and cocci means round balls. Put them together and you get Staphylococci! [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is the protective protein coat that surrounds and shields a virus's genetic material?
explanation: The capsid acts like a tough little security helmet protecting the virus's inner genetic core. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h4)

question: Why is it clinically helpful for nurses and staff to know if a virus is enveloped or non-enveloped?

options.A: It reveals whether the patient has a bacterial co-infection
options.B: It proves the patient requires immediate surgical intervention
options.C: It determines the exact blood pressure medication needed
options.D: It indicates how easily disinfectants can destroy the virus

explanation: Enveloped viruses have a fragile outer fatty layer that makes them super easy to wipe out with standard hospital disinfectants and hand soap! [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which major cell feature do fungi and parasites share that bacteria do not have?
explanation: Unlike bacteria (which are simple prokaryotes), fungi and parasites are eukaryotes—meaning their cells have a proper, well-defined nucleus. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h5)

question: What do we call fungi that can switch between growing as a mold or as a yeast depending on the temperature?
explanation: 'Di' means two, and 'morphic' means shapes! Dimorphic fungi can change their form depending on whether they are in the environment or inside the human body. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h5)

question: What is the main job of the PCR test when identifying microbes?

options.A: Measuring the patient's immune response to a virus
options.B: Amplifying specific segments of microbial DNA
options.C: Staining cell walls purple under a microscope
options.D: Killing resistant fungal spores in the environment

explanation: PCR acts like a genetic photocopier—it takes tiny bits of microbial DNA and multiplies them so the lab can easily spot them. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why are modern molecular tests often preferred over older culture techniques in the lab?

options.A: They require no specialized laboratory equipment whatsoever
options.B: They prevent patients from developing antibiotic allergies
options.C: They provide much faster and more accurate identification
options.D: They completely eliminate the need for trained nurses

explanation: Instead of waiting days for germs to grow in a dish, molecular tests look directly at the pathogen's genes for much quicker results! [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h6)

question: A patient has a confirmed viral chest infection. Why should a nurse question an order for routine antibiotics?

options.A: Antibiotics are ineffective against viral pathogens
options.B: Bacterial stains cannot identify viral cell walls
options.C: Viruses always destroy Gram-positive bacterial flora

explanation: Antibiotics only fight bacteria, not viruses! Giving antibiotics for a viral infection won't help the patient recover. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h7)

question: How does understanding microbial classification help nurses keep the hospital safe?

options.A: It guides the correct selection of isolation precautions and disinfection methods
options.B: It replaces the need for standard hand hygiene protocols
options.C: It determines the patient's daily hospital bed assignment fee
options.D: It dictates the exact visiting hours for family members

explanation: Knowing what kind of germ we are dealing with tells us whether we need contact, droplet, or airborne precautions to protect everyone on the ward. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h7)
